gap: No result ChatGPT got states a measured figure for any candidate. Gidon at The Technology Man measured the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2's AC inverter using about 19 W with nothing plugged in, enough to drain the battery from full to 19% in 12 hours. The measured usable AC energy of the 1 kWh picks is also new: OutdoorGearLab got 950 Wh from the AC180, 910 Wh from the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 and 890 Wh from the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2.
standout_why: I read the three cited rival pages (blackoutwise.com Jackery 1000 v2 + blanket, wattfort.com, and Dealectric's own page) and two uncited top results (runtimemath.com, testedwatts.com). None has a measured figure for any power station. BlackoutWise says 'We do not test units ourselves' and works runtime from 1,070 Wh × 0.85. Tested Watts says 'We don't lab-test power stations (yet)' and assumes a flat 10 W inverter load. RuntimeMath uses Wh × 0.85 and quotes only BLUETTI/Anker's own self-draw figures. WattFort has measured figures only for blankets (from the Cockeyed database), none for stations. ChatGPT's two answers also use flat 85% factors. Our current page already has '19 W measured by one reviewer' for the Elite 30 V2, but it doesn't name the reviewer and has no measured usable Wh for any station.
decides: This confirms the pick and makes the case for it with numbers. The 19 W idle draw measured on the Elite 30 V2 shows that on a 120 V blanket the inverter's own draw is in the same range as the blanket itself, so the Elite 30 V2 should be recommended only for a 12 V blanket on its car port. Among 1 kWh stations, OutdoorGearLab measured the most usable AC energy from the BLUETTI AC180 (950 Wh). StorageReview got 1,030 Wh from it at a 350 W load. That supports keeping the AC180 as the pick for a 120 V blanket, slightly ahead of the Jackery 1000 v2 (910 Wh) and the C1000 Gen 2 and Elite 100 V2 (890 Wh each).

findings.label: AC inverter idle draw (inverter on, no load)
findings.source_title: This $189 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 power station is better than I expected – The Technology Man
findings.note: Gidon (The Technology Man), published 2025-12-23. He left the inverter on with no load and the battery fell from full to 19% in 12 hours, which he reports as 'around 19 W just to keep the inverter running'. Check: 81% × 288 Wh ≈ 233 Wh ÷ 12 h ≈ 19 W. BLUETTI's own figure is 4.5–9 W.

findings.label: Measured usable energy, AC and DC
findings.source_title: This $189 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 power station is better than I expected – The Technology Man
findings.note: Gidon, 2025-12-23, constant AC load (wattage not stated), out of 288 Wh rated. Arithmetic: a 120 V blanket averaging 40 W on low plus about 19 W of inverter overhead is about 59 W, and 231 Wh ÷ 59 W ≈ 3.9 h. This is rough because the 231 Wh figure already includes some inverter loss.
